newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Foreign funds issue mixed calls on Manila shares.
newsitem.headline: Foreign funds issue mixed calls on Manila shares.

text.p: Foreign brokerage houses have issued mixed outlooks for the Philippine equities market, with some warning against steep valuations and a slowdown in corporate earnings and others taking heart in the sliding domestic interest and inflation rates.

The Manila composite index has fallen 13.65 percent or 470.82 points since reaching its all-time high of 3,447.60 on February 3. The steepest daily declines in the 10-week slump were mostly recorded in the past two weeks.

A seven-day losing streak was broken by a mini-rally on Friday, which saw the market gain nearly 28 points to close at 2,976.78 points, but analysts said renewed inflation fears in the U.S. will slam the index again on Monday.
The Dow industrials slumped 148-points on Friday or 2.3 percent after a surprising jump in U.S. wholesale prices.
W.I. Carr research director Christopher Hunt said the securities firm had turned "neutral to underweight" on the Philippine market from "neutral to overweight" since late last year.
"We've been cautious about earnings momentum. We think that earnings growth is slowing down ... And valuation has gotten very, very high," Hunt told Reuters.
He added that many issues had either reached full valuation or, in some property issues, overvaluation during the runup in the last two months of 1996.
Asia Equity Inc chief strategist Ian MacFarlene agreed.

"Our sell view on the market is predicated on valuation and earnings expectations ... Heady earnings expectations of 30 percent, heavily focused on the property sector, mean the only possible surprise is an unpleasant one," MacFarlene said in a report.

The bourse has been dragged down by the property and banking issues. The property sub-index has plummeted 23.29 percent since February 3 while the banking sub-index has skidded 10.47 percent in the past two months.

Fears of a crash in property prices due to a reported oversupply cast a pall of gloom over property issues, while reports of rising bad debts and defaults have sent shudders into already skittish investors.

"Fears of a banking crisis sparked by a collapse in the property market are giving investors, who may have been traumatised by losses in Thailand, anxiety attacks. But is it fair to draw parallels between the two markets? We maintain it is not," Peregrine Securities chief economist Luz Lorenzo said.
Lorenzo said in a report the robust economic growth should spur consumer spending and therefore add to corporate earnings.

"Consequently, both consumer and investment spending should benefit from the lower interest rate environment. Rate sensitive sectors such as banking, construction and property should also do well," she added.

UBS Global Research analyst Norman Villamin said although earnings might be propped up by the lower domestic interest rates, a tighter monetary policy in late 1997 or early 1998 might put a squeeze on corporate margins.

"Current excess liquidity may have inflationary implications moving into 1998 ... To combat inflation, a tighter stance during the second half of 1997 would be prudent. In the absence of an anti-inflation stance, monetary authorities would likely sacrifice currency stability for economic growth," Villamin said.
"As a result, in this environment, we look to further rotate into defensive positions in the market."
All brokerage houses, however, agreed select local shares still offered good value, especially after the recent decline.

"We are beginning to think that there is value emerging in selected stocks ... There should be a flight to quality," W.I. Carr's Hunt said. He said investors should start picking up shares when the index hit 2,800.
